title: Comparison method and pruning the tree
summary: Decide between similar candidates by their key difference, prune irrelevant branches, and stop when a line is good enough — but check for refutations.

steps.md:
## Calculate less, decide better

**Comparison method** (Dvoretsky/Yusupov): when two candidate moves lead to similar positions, do not calculate both to the end. Find the **difference** — a king on g3 instead of f2, a pawn on h3 instead of h2, a rook that is or is not protected — and decide which side the difference favours.

**Pruning** (Kotov, revised by Aagaard):
1. List candidates first; calculate each branch **once**.
2. Calculate only the opponent's **best replies** (forcing ones first).
3. Once you find a line that wins or clearly works, **stop looking for alternatives** and search only for refutations of it ("if you see a good move, look for a better one" applies only when there is time and the position is not yet decided).
4. Stop each line in a **quiet** position and evaluate it.

steps.prompt: White to move. White wants to bring the king to the kingside to support g6 and the h7-rook. Three king moves look similar (Kg3, Kf2, Ke2). Compare them (Capablanca-Tartakower, New York 1924).
steps.hint: Which king move gets to the pawns fastest, and what does the rook capture cost?
steps.explain: **35.Kg3! Rxc3+ 36.Kh4** — Capablanca gives up the c3-pawn: the difference between Kg3 and the "safe" Kf2/Ke2 is that only Kg3 reaches **h5/g6 in time**. White's king supports g6-g7 while the black rook is busy on the queenside; the game went 36...Rf3 37.g6 Rxf4+ 38.Kg5 Re4 39.Kf6 and White won. Engine: +2.3 for Kg3, about +0.3 for Ke2/Kf2.

steps.prompt: White to move. White is a pawn up, but the black rook and bishop are active. Only one king move keeps the advantage (Alekhine-Capablanca, World Championship 1927)
steps.explain: **39.Kh3!** — the king steps out of the bishop's checks and out of ...Rg2-type tricks, keeping all White's pawns protected. Comparing Kh3 with Kf5/Kg5 shows the difference: on h3 the king cannot be checked by the bishop and supports g4/h4. Engine main line: 39.Kh3 Rf2 40.f4 Rf3+ 41.Kg2 Rf2+ 42.Kg1 Rc2. (Alekhine-Capablanca, World Championship 1927; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.prompt: White to move. Compare the king moves: one of them is the only way to keep the balance (Fischer-Spassky, World Championship 1972)
steps.explain: **36.Kh2!** — the king leaves the back rank (no more back-rank checks) and steps off the a7-g1 diagonal of the black bishop. Every other move allows ...Bc5/...Bd6+ with tempo. Engine main line: 36.Kh2 Bd6+ 37.g3 b4 38.Kg2 Ra6 39.f4 Rc6. (Fischer-Spassky, World Championship 1972; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.question: You found a forced line that wins a rook for a knight. Two other candidate moves look promising too. You have 20 minutes left for 15 moves. What do you do?
choices: Calculate both alternatives fully to see if they win more
Check the winning line once more for refutations (in-between moves, checks for the opponent), then play it
steps.explain: Good-enough is enough when the line is clearly winning: spend the time on blunder-checking it, not on finding a prettier win. This is the core of pruning.

steps.question: Two candidate lines both end in a rook ending a pawn up. In line A your king is on e3, in line B it is on e2 and you have an extra tempo. How should you decide?
choices: Calculate both rook endings to mate
Compare only the difference: which matters more, the king one rank further forward or the tempo? Evaluate that and choose
Choose randomly; they are the same
steps.explain: That is the comparison method: identical except for one detail, so evaluate the detail.

steps.md:
## Assignment

- **Calculation drill**: 10 positions at your level in exam mode (no moving pieces, write the full tree with at most 3 candidates per node).
- **Puzzles**: 15 *veryLong* puzzles. After each, count how many branches you calculated that turned out irrelevant.
- In your next long game, note one decision where you used the comparison method; review it after the game.

sources: Dvoretsky & Yusupov, Training for the Tournament Player
